analysis.one_liner: Restores state and local authority to regulate cable TV rates and enforce channel-carrying rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee and never got a vote, dying after cable rates had risen 10.6% in one year versus 4.4% overall inflation.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have undone a 1984 law that barred most state and local governments from regulating cable TV rates. It would let local regulators review and roll back cable prices, including after a cable company rearranged its service tiers, and let governments weigh a company's media ownership when deciding whether to renew its franchise. It also would have required cable systems to keep carrying local broadcast stations to keep their copyright licenses.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers, whose bills had been rising far faster than inflation under regional cable monopolies, would gain a way to contest rates through their state or local franchising authority. Local governments would regain regulatory power stripped by the 1984 Cable Act, and local broadcast stations would gain guaranteed channel placement on cable systems.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the provisions of the 1984 Cable Act that limited state and local authority to regulate cable rates, allowing regulators to set or alter prices starting 180 days after enactment [S3].

It lets a state or franchising authority require rate changes after a cable operator changes service, such as rearranging tiers, with a decision required within 60 days of public notice so customers are not left waiting [S2].

It responds to a problem the bill's own findings document: cable rates rose 10.6% nationally in 1988 while overall inflation was 4.4%, the fastest increase of any category tracked by the Labor Department, and the 1984 law had created regional monopolies [S3].

It lets state and local governments consider a cable operator's ownership of other media when deciding whether to renew a franchise or approve a transfer of control, a check on media concentration [S3].

It conditions cable systems' compulsory copyright license on carrying local broadcast stations on the same channels they occupied in 1985, protecting free over-the-air television's reach into cable homes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators, who had enjoyed six years free of most rate regulation, would bear the cost of rate reviews and potential rollbacks, restrictions tied to their other media holdings, and mandatory carriage of local broadcast channels. Indirectly, if rate pressure slowed investment, cable customers could see slower system upgrades.

drawbacks.text: The 1984 Cable Act was written to promote competition and reduce the economic burden of regulation on cable systems; reattaching rate regulation to regional monopolies could slow investment in cable plant and new programming at a time when the industry was still building out [S3].

The must-carry provisions would force cable systems to dedicate basic-tier channels to broadcast stations whether or not subscribers wanted those channels, consuming capacity that cable operators could otherwise use for new networks [S2].

Allowing governments to block cable operators over their ownership of other media, even if enforcement is limited to renewal and transfer decisions, adds a test of who owns what that goes beyond price and service quality [S3].
The bill relied on local franchising authorities to police rates, and their capacity and diligence varied widely, so protection would depend on where a subscriber lived.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For subscribers in monopoly cable markets, the prospect of local rate review was a direct answer to price increases running more than double the inflation rate, and the 60-day decision deadline kept the process from dragging on. The costs fell on cable companies rather than on other taxpayers, though weaker investment incentives and mandatory channel carriage were real trade-offs. On balance the bill's benefits to consumers plausibly outweighed its costs, but it was never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Lieberman introduced the bill on May 3, 1989, with findings that cable rates had risen 10.6% the prior year against 4.4% overall inflation and that the 1984 deregulation had created regional monopolies [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; no further action of any kind appears in its history [S5].
It attracted only one cosponsor in the 55-member Senate Democratic caucus [S4].
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, with the bill still sitting in committee, so it died without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators kept the rate deregulation they had won in 1984, with no local review of prices, no ownership conditions at franchise renewal, and no new must-carry obligations. Cable subscribers continued paying the fastest-rising prices of any tracked service category with no local recourse.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regional cable monopolies kept rate freedom

for.name: Joseph I. Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as sole sponsor

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from May 1989 until the Congress ended without a hearing, markup, or vote

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote and no recorded opposition exists, so its partisan shape cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the rate-deregulation shield the 1984 Cable Act gave cable systems, exposing prices to state and local review and tying franchise renewals to ownership conditions. Its own findings called the 1984 framework a creator of regional monopolies, so the bill targeted the industry's core pricing power [S3].

Must-carry conditions on the compulsory copyright license would guarantee broadcast stations their cable channel positions, keeping free over-the-air television visible to cable subscribers. This aligned broadcasters with cable customers against cable operators [S2].

The bill restored regulatory authority stripped in 1984, giving these governments power over rates, tier changes, and franchise renewal decisions. They are governments rather than an industry, but they were direct beneficiaries of the shift [S2].
